title: Describing things
goal: Use adjectives in their three forms, and understand double definiteness — the pattern that makes Swedish say "the" twice in a single phrase.
bekal: the three forms of an adjective: *stor*, *stort*, *stora*
the most common adjectives, and the irregular ones

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Den gröna ryggsäcken
dialogs.intro: A backpack has been left behind in the reading room of the university library. Dian takes it to the front desk.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Hej, jag hittade en ryggsäck i läsesalen.
lines.id: Hi, I found a backpack in the reading room.
lines.literal: hi, I found a backpack in reading-room-the.

lines.speaker: Personalen:
lines.id: Thanks! What does it look like?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Den är grön och ganska stor. Den har en gul rand.
lines.id: It's green and fairly big. It has a yellow stripe.
lines.literal: it is green and fairly big. it has a yellow stripe.

lines.speaker: Personalen:
lines.text: Den stora gröna ryggsäcken? Den har någon frågat efter.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad bra. Är det en student?

notes: **Den stora gröna ryggsäcken** says "the" **twice**: once in front as *den*, once at the end as the ending *-en* — literally "the big green backpack-the". This is **double definiteness**, and it is a hallmark of Swedish; Danish, for example, does without it. To an English ear it sounds like one "the" too many, but leave either one out and the phrase sounds broken.

**An adjective in a definite phrase always ends in *-a***, whatever the gender and number of the noun: *den stor**a** bilen*, *det stor**a** huset*, *de stor**a** bilarna*. That saves memorizing — the only tricky part is the indefinite phrase.

**Liten is the only truly irregular adjective**: *en liten bil*, *ett litet hus*, *små bilar*, *den lilla bilen*, *de små bilarna*. Four forms that don't even look alike. It is also one of the most frequent words, so you will learn it simply by using it.

**Gammal** loses a letter when it gets an ending: *en gammal bil* → *den gamla bilen*, *gamla bilar*. The same pattern applies to *vacker* → *vackra* and *enkel* → *enkla*. This is a sound adjustment, not a random exception.

**En kille** means "guy", and its partner *en tjej* means "girl, gal" (pronounced **shay**). Both are everyday words; the neutral forms are *en man* and *en kvinna*, while *en pojke* and *en flicka* are for children. Calling a twenty-year-old student a *pojke* sounds odd — like calling him a "little boy".

**Väldigt** means "very, really" and in conversation is much more common than *mycket* in front of an adjective. Its cousins: *jättebra* (super good), *jättestor* (huge) — the prefix *jätte-* literally means "giant", and it attaches to any adjective, much like English *super-*.

grammars.title: The three forms of an adjective
after: The fifth row is easy to miss: an adjective standing **after the verb** (*är*, *blir*, *verkar*) never takes the *-a* ending in the singular. *Bilen är stor*, *Huset är stort*, *Bilarna är stora*. What decides is still the gender and number of the noun — English adjectives never change at all, so this is the part that needs practice.
The last row matters too: after *min*, *din*, *hans* or a name ending in *-s*, the adjective takes the *-a* form even without *den*. *Min stora bil*, *Elins nya jacka*, *hans gamla dator*.
Adjectives that **already end in *-t*** don't change for *ett*-words: *svart* stays *svart*. Those ending in a long vowel double the *t*: *blå* → *blått*, *ny* → *nytt*, *fri* → *fritt*.

grammars.title: Irregular adjectives
after: **Bra never changes** in any form: *en bra bok*, *ett bra hus*, *bra böcker*, *den bra boken*. It is one of a handful of adjectives free of every rule on this page, and luckily it is also one of the most used.
**Liten/lilla/små** needs attention: *lilla* is used in the definite singular (*den lilla bilen*), while *små* is for the plural (*små bilar*, *de små bilarna*). There is no form *litena* or *litna*.

blocks.text: **Lätt** does two jobs: "easy" and "light". So it has two opposites: *svår* (difficult) and *tung* (heavy). Context tells them apart. English splits this into two words — though "light work" shows the same overlap is there in English too.
After double definiteness, one more pattern that works the same way: the demonstratives "this" and "that".

Notice the third row: the formal *denna/detta/dessa* takes the **indefinite** noun (*denna bil*, not *denna bilen*), while *den här* takes the **definite** form (*den här bilen*, literally "the here car-the"). The formal version is used in official writing and the news; in conversation, *den här* wins hands down.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 10
items: Explain to yourself, in one sentence, the difference between *sin* and *hans*.
Then combine it with this unit's adjectives: *Han tog sin gamla cykel*, *Hon ringde sin snälla mamma*, *De städade sina små rum*.
Notice that an adjective after *sin/min/hans* always takes the *-a* form, with no need for *den* in front.
